newsitem.title: USA: Polling shows most Americans back NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Polling shows most Americans back NATO expansion.

text.p: President Bill Clinton has made NATO expansion a major foreign policy goal in his hoped-for second term and, while the idea has some formidable opponents, polling shows most Americans support it.

Last week Clinton used the only foreign policy speech of his re-election campaign to spotlight NATO expansion plans, elevating the issue to the front and centre of his global strategy and doubtless his drive for the history books.

Clinton told a crowd in Detroit that NATO should move to consolidate democracy in post-Cold War Europe by admitting new members by 1999. He did not say which countries should join the western military alliance first, but conventional allied wisdom says it will be the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.
The New York Times riposted with a headline three days later declaring that it was the "Wrong Time to Expand NATO."

The Times editorial said enlarging the 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, formed in 1949 to contain Soviet power, could "drive Russia into an aggrieved corner," provoking the Kremlin hostility the West wants to avoid.
This echoed the concerns of some members of Congress, where the Senate must approve any treaty expanding NATO. But the White House did not appear overly worried.
Clinton aides were encouraged by a recent poll that said 62 percent of Americans supported expanding NATO to include countries such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
The poll said support was "fairly resilient," but did "soften" when respondents were told about possible costs and the potential for the commitment to lead to nuclear conflict.
The survey of 1,214 adults was conducted September 14-20 by the University of Maryland's Programme on International Policy Attitudes. The margin of error is 3 percent to 4 percent.
"The poll suggests that Clinton's (NATO) agenda is going to be pretty easy," said Steven Kull, the principal poll investigator. "There isn't any significant resistance."

"This vindicates our judgment," a senior administration official said of the poll. "It validates our view that the American people want an integrated Europe rooted in democracy and security ... NATO enlargement is a means to that end."

Meanwhile the poll startled critics of NATO expansion plans. "I was suprised by the numbers in the sense that they were more positive than I expected," said Charles Kupchan, a former Clinton White House official who is now a senior fellow for Europe on the Council on Foreign Relations.
But he thought the public was largely unaware of the issue and would be more apprehensive once the risks were known.

Indeed the poll said only a plurality of 46 percent thought NATO expansion would be "worth the cost" if it cost $1 billion a year over and above the current defence budget, and just 44 percent would favour expansion if it meant committing to using nuclear arms to defend new members.
"Seeing those sorts of (polling) numbers makes me feel like it (NATO expansion) may happen, but the domestic battle is still going to be fierce," Kupchan said.

A NATO summit in 1997 is expected to name the first candidates for membership and lead to negotiations. Then each NATO country must ratify the treaties with new members, a process that could start with the Senate as soon as 1998, if Clinton's 1999 target date for expansion is to be met.

Clinton's political opponents were not lining up against NATO expansion. In fact many Republicans, including presidential contender Bob Dole, said Clinton was not moving fast enough, and NATO should take in new members by 1998.
Some of the more notable Senate critics of expansion, like Georgia Democrat Sam Nunn, have announced their retirement this year.

But Jeremy Rosner, a senior associate at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said Senate approval could not be taken for granted, noting that since the Cold War ended Congress had been more volatile on foreign policy.
He said Clinton would have to be careful to make NATO expansion a bipartisan goal and draw Congress into the process, perhaps even during negotiations with new members.
"If this becomes seen as a political win for Clinton, a lot of Republicans might peel off," said Rosner, who is also a former White House official.

The stakes were high and opponents could be well-organised, he said. "This will be a huge decision, making a treaty commitment to these countries to protect them at all and any cost. We don't do that often."
